Asset redesign
01 Problem 02 Constraints 03 Decisions 04 How I worked 05 The turn 06 Outcome 07 Web 08 Reflection Back to top

A redesign of the asset page — the home of the Asset tab — for a platform where people trade both crypto and US stocks. The project had been stuck for almost two years, and when it finally moved the brief was one line: “it looks messy.”

My job was to turn that into a clear problem, a shippable hierarchy, and a decision the team could align on in a week. Three months and five new features later, the same structure was still carrying all of them — the part of this case I trust most.

01 · Problem & diagnosis

Why the first task was diagnosis, not layout

Three conditions came with the brief, and each one shaped what an answer could look like.

  • Ship fast, on limited resources, with no compromise on the experience. That was the whole bar.
  • Merge the two holdings sections, so people could tell what they actually owned. That was leadership’s only specific instruction.
  • Nothing would be built until the direction cleared review. Engineering hadn’t started, so what I owed was a call the team could commit to, not a vision that would stall again.

What was actually broken

“Messy” is a feeling, not a problem. Stated as the user’s: someone with several accounts could not answer “how am I doing?” without reading four blocks and doing the arithmetic themselves. Underneath that, four layers were talking at once. In order, they should have read:

  1. 1Total assets — one number that answers “how am I doing?”
  2. 2Account — which of my accounts I am looking at, driving every figure below
  3. 3Crypto / Securities → holdings — what I own, in one structure for both
  4. 4Detail on demand — margin, positions, market context, behind a tap
On the screen to the left: flat weight · duplicated numbers · a split mental model · no reading path.
In one sentence The screen didn’t look messy by accident. Its information architecture was broken. Every later decision had one filter: does this clarify hierarchy, or just rearrange the noise?
02 · Constraints & trade-offs

Why there was no template to copy

Three forces on one small screen. The obvious references — the top crypto exchanges and the established brokerage apps — had each solved for one of them, and none of their answers transferred.

Account ·· 1135 ▾1
CryptoSecurities2
Borrow against crypto →3
  1. 1

    Multi-account, surfaced not buried

    Other exchanges bury the account switcher in settings — fine when most people hold one account. Ours ran several at once, so the switcher had to sit on the page and drive every figure below it.

  2. 2

    Two pattern languages, one screen

    Crypto apps and brokerages have trained their users on different conventions. Most products pick a side; this one carried both from day one, so the page had to feel familiar arriving from either habit.

  3. 3

    A new product still explaining itself

    Incumbents can afford calm, spacious screens; nobody needs telling what they do. A new product has to argue for itself here too — without sliding back into the density we came to fix.

Every decision was a trade-off

A management review to clear, and no engineering resourced yet — none of the ideal answers were free.

Fix the hierarchy without touching the data model

ChoseA clearer reading order, built from fields that already existed
over
Gave upAnything that needed a new API

Cost — some ideas from the exploration could not be built. Engineering was not resourced yet, so a design that needed new endpoints would have waited for a team that did not exist. This one shipped in two weeks.

One structure for crypto and securities

ChoseBoth asset classes reading the same way
over
Gave upThe crypto-native layout its users already knew

Cost — crypto users had to relearn a screen they knew. Securities ran on a third-party interface that was expensive to change, so alignment could only come from the crypto side. How it was built is decision 02.

A calm first screen

ChoseProtecting the reading path
over
Gave upMarketing’s financing offers above the fold

Cost — the growth team lost its most valuable placement. Financing moved below the fold, where it still converts but more slowly — a real price, paid to keep the page answering its first question first.

Decision 01

Start with Net Worth / total assets

One large number + change up top — answer “how am I doing?” first.

Decision 02

Collapse account hierarchy into one path

Why: Smallest change that fixed the split mental model without a new data contract.

Decision 03

Move the risk numbers off the first screen

The margin ratios — IMR and MMR, the two numbers that decide whether you get liquidated — plus the dense overview rows and the promo banners, all move one screen down. Nothing is deleted; they just stop competing with the headline for the same glance.

Why: Every one of those numbers was correct. The problem was that they were the same size and the same weight as “how much do I have,” so the eye had no idea which to read first. A sequencing problem, not a content problem.

Decision 04

Progressive detail disclosure

Positions, margin, and market context expand on demand.

Why: Traders still need depth — just not all at once.

04 · How I worked

One week, a clickable prototype almost every day

The differentiator wasn’t just speed, it was the medium. Every day the founders, the CEO and the management team opened a clickable HTML prototype with realistic data, not a static Figma frame. They could feel the hierarchy, tap the account switch, and argue about a real experience. That compressed two years of ambiguity into one week of decisions.

17Saved prototype versions between 14 and 20 May — every one of them clickable, with realistic data.
2 yrsHow long the project had been stalled before this sprint.
1 wkFrom restart to leadership alignment on the hierarchy.

One prototype per day, captured on the asset tab from the saved files. 15 May has no prototype — it went to a competitor teardown, not pixels. The prototypes were built in zh-CN and are shown here with the product’s own English strings; the last frame is the live build.

What a round of that loop actually changed

Decision 02 — keeping the hierarchy readable after you switch between crypto and securities

“One card per account, with a Crypto / Securities switch” is the conclusion. It took three builds to get there, and each one failed at something specific.

See the three builds it took, and what each one got wrong — 16, 19, 20 May
  • 1Where the switch lives — Gen 1 selects by tapping a card; Gen 2 moves it to a segmented control; Gen 3 keeps the control and folds the accounts under the number.
  • 2What the panel holds — Gen 1 stacks rings and bars; Gen 2 fits the real fields; Gen 3 makes the account split an expandable line that adds up to the headline.
  • 3What was outside the panel — Gen 2 dropped the account cards below; Gen 3 brings them inside — and the credit line, new since the pivot, sits where borrowing used to.

Three builds of the same decision inside the sprint week: 16 May → 19 May → 20 May. Gen 3 is the version we aligned on; the frame is captured from today’s build, which is why it carries the credit line added later. Demo data.

The other directions I explored

The version we didn’t ship — mocked up with AI so the team could try it before deciding

Before locking the shippable direction I mocked up the most ambitious version of the page as a clickable prototype — AI-assisted, no engineering time, a few hours of mine. Not a leftover ideal: the cheapest way to make the cost of each trade-off concrete for the people deciding.

  • Net worth, not just total. Led with total assets − borrowed and a 30-day trend — the number high-net-worth users actually track.
  • Multi-account aggregation. Combine selected accounts into one net-worth, borrowed, and buying-power view — the multi-account constraint, solved directly.
  • Asset-class breakdown. Crypto and securities in one proportional read, each expandable, so both kinds of trader find their world fast.
  • Financing & liquidity. Surfaced “how much can I borrow,” buying power, and one-tap repay — the marketing ask, made genuinely useful.
What exploration bought us One week of alignment, two of build — because the cost of each trade-off was on the table, clickable, while the decision was being made. Interactive demo — tap the account name, toggle “Combine accounts,” and expand “Financing & liquidity.” Demo data.
05 · The turn

The review kept the structure and took the layering

The review came back in two parts, and they landed at different layers.

  • Leadership approved the hierarchy, and was specific about why: crypto and securities finally read as one aligned layout; the account switch had a visible relationship to the content it drove; and — the line I cared about most — holdings and coin balances had stopped being two separate things, which is the concrete ask leadership opened with in 01, answered.
  • The design lead’s note landed at the surface. Not a rejection of the direction — a reshaping of how it looked. Three things went, and each one bought something.

Crypto tab: before and after the review

  • 1Dark layering behind the hero — separated the account world from the page. Bought: one visual language instead of two, and a dark mode that costs a fraction to build.
  • 2Buttons in their own accent colours — each action had its own hue. Bought: buttons inherit the global palette, still being decided then, so nothing here had to be re-decided later.
  • 3Card layer beneath the account tabs — bound the switch to the content it drives. Bought: a calmer, more uniform page — paid for with a weaker link between the switch and its numbers. The one I’d still argue for.

Crypto tab, before and after the review. The information architecture is identical in both — every change is at the surface. Design boards captured in the product’s original zh-CN; there was never an English version of these two.

Securities tab

Securities tab — the same trade applied consistently. Structure intact, layering gone. Design boards captured in zh-CN.

The trade, stated plainly I traded visual hierarchy for consistency and an affordable dark mode.
  • The card layer under the account tabs is the one I’d still argue for. Of the three removals it is the only one carrying meaning rather than style.
  • Consistency across every screen is a system-level call, not a page-level one. The design lead saw further across the product than one page’s designer could — it was the right call for him to make.
  • The information architecture went through untouched. That was the layer I was accountable for, and it is why the audit in 06 reads the way it does.
06 · Outcome

Three months later the product had changed. The structure hadn’t.

  • Leadership aligned on the information hierarchy and approved the redesign to move into implementation — after almost two years stalled.
  • Then the product kept growing underneath it. Over the following months the same page absorbed a second fiat currency, a full risk-control system, yield promoted to a headline feature, Hong Kong stocks alongside US, and credit that moves both ways between crypto and securities. Separately, our design leader ran a company-wide design-system unification.
  • I owned the asset design throughout. So this is not a story about someone else preserving my work. It is that feature after feature arrived and the structure kept taking them: a second fiat currency, a full risk-control system, yield promoted to a headline, Hong Kong stocks, two-way credit — each one found a place inside the existing four layers instead of forcing a new one. That is what robust and scalable means here: not that the structure was defended, but that it kept having room.

Three months on, I put the two builds side by side and audited them layer by layer. The visual language had been replaced and the scope had grown considerably. The load-bearing structure was untouched.

  • 1Total assets with its trend — one headline number, one line. Kept
  • 2The account and its P&L — the switcher drives every figure below it. Deepened more account types, a donut, multi-select aggregation.
  • 3Recent records — three rows, then the list. Kept detail still one tap down.
  • 4The asset-class switch — same control, one structure for both. Kept order flipped to put securities first.
  • 5Net assets and the accounts that add up to it — the distribution expands under the number in both. Kept

The same tab, three months apart. Read them top-down and the numbered order is identical, line for line. What changed is surface and scope: an entirely replaced visual language, the asset-class order flipped to put securities first, and a two-way credit system (a credit in figure and its transfer entry) that did not exist at alignment. Left board captured in zh-CN; right is the live build in English.

See the three things the product grew around the spine afterwards

Three things the product grew afterwards

These do not show up in the comparison above, because they are not part of the four layers — they grew alongside them. Each one repeats the same call: answer first, detail later.

  • The “Add assets” entry point. At alignment it collapsed four scattered actions into one. Today it is one sheet, three cards, and guidance when cash is short — the same single entry, carrying more cases.
  • Idle-balance yield. At alignment it was scattered across four places. Today it is one hero card, four data cells and three states, promoted to the top — a scattered feature turned into one readable block.
  • “Hide small balances.” Three months on, not one character has changed. A small thing — but it means the wording was already right.
Why this is the evidence I trust It took on five features it was never drawn for, and the reading order never changed. That is not something a presentation can produce; it can only come from the structure itself — which is what tells me those early calls were structural rather than decorative.
07 · Web

One mental model, two screens

The web redesign was not about making the web nicer. The goal was that the same person sees the same thing on a phone and on a desktop — same order, same controls, same words.

  • High-net-worth users live in the app. They use the web far less, so the problem definition, the exploration and the review all happened on the app side — and web inherited the conclusion rather than re-deriving it.
  • One board with both screens on it, reviewed together. Not two proposals — one question: do these two screens read in the same order? That is what made the decision quick.
  • A wide screen changes the density, not the order. It fits more at once, so “one tap down” on the phone becomes “the column on the right” on the desktop.

08 · Reflection

What I’d carry forward, and what I’d change

This case was built to do one thing: take a screen that had been stalled for two years and get it to a decision the team could commit to, inside a week. Here is the scope it ran in, and what I take from it.

What I owned

  • ✓ Information architecture
  • ✓ Prioritization & reading path
  • ✓ Interaction design
  • ✓ Clickable HTML prototypes & daily stakeholder loop

Owned by others

  • · Product strategy
  • · Timeline / release window
  • · Engineering resources
  • · Research budget

Three things I’d do again

  • A clickable prototype every day. Real data, real taps. It turned two years of circular discussion into a week of decisions — next time I would still reach for a prototype before a deck.
  • Name the structure before touching the layout. Once “messy” became four named layers, every later decision had one test: does this clarify the hierarchy, or just rearrange it?
  • Close debt with rules, not patches. I fixed the scroll-rhythm problem with two rules rather than case-by-case tweaks — they keep working when I am no longer looking at the page.
Looking back — three things I’d change
  • Pick one number and track it from day one. Something as plain as “how long does it take someone to find their own total?” I argued the new structure was clearer and I was right, but I could only say so — not show it. Nobody refused me that number; I never asked for it.
  • Argue the upside, not only the price. I used the ambitious prototype to show what each trade-off would cost us. I never used it to show what the bigger version would have been worth. Showing the cost got the shippable version approved; showing the value might have got a more ambitious one through as well.
  • Give the good ideas a date. The stronger ideas from the exploration are still unbuilt — not because anyone rejected them, but because nothing ever said when. A named phase two would have kept them alive instead of leaving them in a folder.
The outcome I value most isn’t the UI anyway. It’s creating clarity in a project that had been blocked for two years, and building it solidly enough that it kept holding as the product grew.
What this case doesn’t show

Research and measurement were not in this project’s conditions. The other half of the practice is in these two.
